claim: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) convert increased extracellular proton concentrations during neurotransmission to excitatory sodium influx.
source: Increased extracellular proton concentrations during neurotransmission are converted to excitatory sodium influx by acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Du et al., 2014; Kreple et al., 2014).

claim: ASICs exhibit approximately 10-fold sodium/potassium selectivity.
source: 10-fold sodium/potassium selectivity in ASICs has long been attributed to a central constriction in the channel pore
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and further supported in the introduction with citations (Gründer and Pusch, 2015; Waldmann et al., 1997).

claim: The GAS belt does not show preference for sodium ions over potassium ions.
source: We observed no preference for sodium at the "GAS belt" in the central constriction.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A band of glutamate and aspartate side chains at the lower end of the pore enables preferential sodium conduction.
source: Instead, we identified a band of glutamate and aspartate side chains at the lower end of the pore that enables preferential sodium conduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4 and MD simulations in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: ASIC1a is widely expressed in the mammalian nervous system, notably the brain.
source: The prototypical example, ASIC1a, is widely expressed in the mammalian nervous system, notably the brain, where it is involved in learning, memory and anxiety (Pidoplichko et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Ziemann et al., 2009) and neuroinflammation and ischemia (Voilley et al., 2001; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASIC1a is involved in learning, memory and anxiety.
source: The prototypical example, ASIC1a, is widely expressed in the mammalian nervous system, notably the brain, where it is involved in learning, memory and anxiety (Pidoplichko et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Ziemann et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: ASIC1a is involved in neuroinflammation and ischemia.
source: where it is involved in learning, memory and anxiety (Pidoplichko et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Ziemann et al., 2009) and neuroinflammation and ischemia (Voilley et al., 2001; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: ASIC1a, in concert with ASIC2a and ASIC3, mediates pain and nociception in central and peripheral neurons.
source: In central and peripheral neurons, ASIC1a, in concert with ASIC2a and ASIC3, mediates pain and nociception, drawing much attention as a pharmacological target for novel analgesics (Baron and Lingueglia, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: ASICs are excitatory because of approximately 10-fold selectivity for Na+ over K+.
source: ASICs are excitatory because of approximately 10-fold selectivity for Na+ over potassium (K+; [Gründer and Pusch, 2015; Waldmann et al., 1997])
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The 10-fold Na+/K+ selectivity is conserved in most vertebrate members of the DEG/ENaC family of channels.
source: ASICs are excitatory because of approximately 10-fold selectivity for Na+ over potassium (K+; [Gründer and Pusch, 2015; Waldmann et al., 1997]), a feature conserved in most vertebrate members of the overarching DEG/ENaC family of channels
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Mutation of the G-X-S motif in ENaCs affects ion selectivity and increases permeation of larger cations.
source: Experiments on heteromeric ENaCs have shown effects on ion selectivity and greater permeation of larger cations upon mutation of a highly conserved G-X-S motif in the pore-forming helix, suggestive of a size exclusion filter (Kellenberger et al., 1999a; Snyder et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The GAS belt forms a constriction half-way down the pore in an X-ray structure of chick ASIC1 in a putative open-channel state.
source: By homology, this idea naturally extended to ASICs (Kellenberger and Schild, 2002), receiving recent support from the presence of a constriction half-way down the pore in an X-ray structure of chick ASIC1 in a putative open-channel state (Baconguis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to structural data.

claim: The GAS belt constriction is formed by G-A-S motifs from each of three adjacent subunits in ASIC1a.
source: In ASIC1a, the constriction is formed by G-A-S motifs from each of three adjacent subunits, suggesting that this 'GAS belt' forms the ASIC selectivity filter, presumably favoring Na+ by excluding larger K+ ions (Baconguis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to structural data.

claim: Mutation of G10' and S12' residues renders homomeric ASICs non-functional.
source: Unfortunately, the role of the GAS belt in ion selectivity lacks experimental verification, as the mutation of presumed critical G10' and S12' residues (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for numbering) renders homomeric ASICs non-functional (Carattino and Della Vecchia, 2012; Li et al., 2011b; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Selective Na+ conduction has been ascribed to G10' main chain carbonyl oxygen atoms that point into the pore.
source: Moreover, selective Na+ conduction has been ascribed to G10' main chain carbonyl oxygen atoms that point into the pore (Baconguis et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: A11'α substitution replaces the G10' main chain amide carbonyl with an ester carbonyl.
source: We used in vivo nonsense suppression (Dougherty and Van Arnam, 2014) to replace A11' with its α-hydroxy analogue ('α') in ASIC1a channels expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes (Figure 1A,B). This replaces the G10' main chain amide carbonyl with an ester carbonyl
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A11'α substitution decreases the backbone dipole and electrostatic surface potential near the G10' carbonyl oxygen.
source: This replaces the G10' main chain amide carbonyl with an ester carbonyl, decreasing the backbone dipole and thus the electrostatic surface potential near the G10' carbonyl oxygen (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: A11'α substitution has little effect on general channel function.
source: Unlike substitution via conventional mutagenesis of the GAS belt in ASICs, this substitution had remarkably little effect on general channel function, evident in unaltered proton-gated currents at A11'α channels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Na+ conductance through A11'α channels is indistinguishable from wild-type.
source: To test if ion conduction was affected, we pulled outside-out patches and measured single channel Na+ currents through A11'α channels and observed that Na+ conductance was indistinguishable from wild-type (WT), despite the significant alteration of the G10' carbonyl oxygen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single channel data in Figure 1D.

claim: A11'α channels maintain high, WT-like levels of Na+ selectivity over K+ and Cs+.
source: A11'α channels maintained high, WT-like levels of Na+ selectivity over the larger K+ and Cs+ (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: A11'α channels show an increase in PNa+/PK+ compared to wild-type.
source: A11'α channels maintained high, WT-like levels of Na+ selectivity over the larger K+ and Cs+ (Figure 1E), with an increase in PNa+/PK+ that signifies interactions with G10' specific to K+ conductance
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: MD simulations show no free energy preference for Na+ ions at the GAS belt.
source: We observed no free energy preference for Na+ ions at the GAS belt (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by free energy profiles in Figure 2B.

claim: Independent calculations of relative binding free energy confirm no preference for Na+ at the GAS belt.
source: We observed no free energy preference for Na+ ions at the GAS belt (Figure 2B), which was confirmed by independent calculations of relative binding free energy at this part of the channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FEP calculations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both Na+ and K+ maintain their solvation shell when passing the GAS belt.
source: When passing the GAS belt, both Na+ and K+ maintain their solvation shell, but K+ ions do so with more contribution from the protein, interacting with G10' amide carbonyl oxygen atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by coordination analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: K+ ions interact with G10' amide carbonyl oxygen atoms when passing the GAS belt.
source: When passing the GAS belt, both Na+ and K+ maintain their solvation shell, but K+ ions do so with more contribution from the protein, interacting with G10' amide carbonyl oxygen atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by coordination analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Free energy differences between Na+ and K+ are observed at L7' and E18'-D21'.
source: Free energy differences between Na+ and K+ were observed at L7' and E18'-D21' (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by free energy profiles in Figure 2B.

claim: K+ undergoes partial dehydration without sufficient compensation by backbone carbonyls around L7'.
source: These results are explained by partial dehydration of K+ without sufficient compensation by backbone carbonyls around L7' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by coordination analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Na+ exhibits high field strength binding to negative charge at E18'-D21'.
source: These results are explained by partial dehydration of K+ without sufficient compensation by backbone carbonyls around L7' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and high field strength binding (Hille, 1972) of Na+ to negative charge at E18'-D21'.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Independent binding calculations demonstrate a relative Na+/K+ stability of 1.4 ± 0.1 kcal/mol for binding at E18'.
source: Furthermore, independent binding calculations have demonstrated a relative Na+/K+ stability of 1.4 ± 0.1 kcal/mol for binding at E18' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FEP calculations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Simulations reveal formation of complexes with 1–2 ions and 1–2 carboxylate groups involving E18' and D21'.
source: Simulations with NaCl or KCl also revealed formation of complexes with 1–2 ions and 1–2 carboxylate groups, involving E18' and D21' (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by occupancy analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Single ion occupancy dominates for both Na+ and K+ at E18'/D21'.
source: Although single ion occupancy dominates for both Na+ and K+, double ion occupancy occurred more frequently for Na+ (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by occupancy analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Double ion occupancy at E18'/D21' occurs more frequently for Na+ than K+.
source: Although single ion occupancy dominates for both Na+ and K+, double ion occupancy occurred more frequently for Na+ (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by occupancy analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The doubly occupied site at E18'/D21' is 3.0 ± 0.4 kcal/mol more stable for Na+ than for K+.
source: and this doubly occupied site was 3.0 ± 0.4 kcal/mol more stable for Na+ than for K+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FEP calculations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: E18'/D21' is a likely site to increase Na+ concentration in a selective multi-ion permeation mechanism.
source: Thus, simulations identify E18'/D21' as a likely site to increase Na+ concentration in a selective multi-ion permeation mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation data.

claim: The lower pore of PDB:4NTW is noticeably splayed.
source: However, the lower pore of this apparently open chick ASIC1/snake toxin complex (PDB:4NTW) is noticeably splayed (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The splayed lower pore in PDB:4NTW may be a consequence of the removal of intracellular N- and C-termini for crystallization.
source: However, the lower pore of this apparently open chick ASIC1/snake toxin complex (PDB:4NTW) is noticeably splayed (Figure 3A), possibly as a consequence of the removal of intracellular N- and C-termini for crystallization (Baconguis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with a supporting citation.

claim: Parts of the intracellular N- and C-terminal regions help form the conducting pore in ASICs.
source: We note that parts of these intracellular regions help form the conducting pore (Pfister et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Parts of the intracellular N- and C-terminal regions affect efficiency of channel opening in ASICs.
source: We note that parts of these intracellular regions help form the conducting pore (Pfister et al., 2006) and affect efficiency of channel opening (Jing et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016) in ASICs
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Intracellular regions make crucial contributions to gating and ion conduction in other trimeric ion channels.
source: and also make crucial contributions to gating and ion conduction in other trimeric ion channels (Gründer et al., 1999; Mansoor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: PDB:2QTS shows a significantly narrower lower channel pore than PDB:4NTW.
source: In the absence of such an ASIC structure, we examined ion binding to PDB:2QTS (Jasti et al., 2007), a closed-channel chick ASIC1 X-ray structure which resolves an additional 10 lower pore residues and shows a significantly narrower lower channel pore (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Simulations with PDB:2QTS reveal preferential binding of a single Na+ ion by up to 2.6 ± 0.3 kcal/mol near E18'.
source: These simulations revealed preferential binding of a single Na+ ion by up to 2.6 ± 0.3 kcal/mol near E18' (Figure 3B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by free energy calculations in Figure 3B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the narrower pore structure of PDB:2QTS, predominant formation of double ion complexes with E18' and/or D21' from neighboring subunits is observed.
source: In this narrower pore structure, we observed predominant formation of double ion complexes with E18' and/or D21' from neighboring subunits (Figure 3C, left graph)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by occupancy analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: A greater proportion of tightly bound complexes at E18'/D21' is observed for Na+ in PDB:2QTS.
source: In this narrower pore structure, we observed predominant formation of double ion complexes with E18' and/or D21' from neighboring subunits (Figure 3C, left graph), with a greater proportion of tightly bound complexes for Na+ (right graph).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by occupancy analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Cooperative complex formation at E18'/D21' in PDB:2QTS leads to a significant 5.9 ± 0.6 kcal/mol preference for Na+ over K+.
source: Such cooperative complex formation leads to a significant 5.9 ± 0.6 kcal/mol preference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), aggressively favoring Na+ ions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FEP calculations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: L7', L14', E18' and D21' are the only residues whose mutation markedly altered ion selectivity among 16 pore-forming positions tested.
source: We therefore measured relative ion permeabilities in a series of mutants involving 16 additional pore-forming positions and found that L7', L14', E18' and D21' were the only residues whose mutation markedly altered ion selectivity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4A.

claim: Only substantial changes in L7' side chain size/length dramatically altered selectivity.
source: Regarding L7', it was only substantial changes in side chain size/length that dramatically altered selectivity, with L7'I and even L7'V substitutions not decreasing Na+/K+ selectivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both E18'Q and E18'D mutations abolished selectivity.
source: The fact that both E18'Q and E18'D mutations abolished selectivity (Figure 4A) suggests that both side chain charge and length make important contributions to Na+ conduction at this position.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4A.

claim: Both side chain charge and length of E18' make important contributions to Na+ conduction.
source: The fact that both E18'Q and E18'D mutations abolished selectivity (Figure 4A) suggests that both side chain charge and length make important contributions to Na+ conduction at this position.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the mutagenesis data in Figure 4A.

claim: PNa+/PK+ is reduced to unity for E18'€ channels.
source: Although currents at oocytes expressing E18'€ channels were relatively small (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we could measure approximate reversal potentials for Na+ and K+ and establish that PNa+/PK+ was reduced to unity for E18'€ (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: E18' negative charge is essential for Na+ selectivity.
source: Although currents at oocytes expressing E18'€ channels were relatively small (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we could measure approximate reversal potentials for Na+ and K+ and establish that PNa+/PK+ was reduced to unity for E18'€ (Figure 4B), thus verifying that E18' negative charge is essential for Na+ selectivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the E18'€ data in Figure 4B.

claim: Single channel activity through E18'D channels is significantly reduced compared to wild-type.
source: Moreover, single channel activity through E18'D channels was significantly reduced (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single channel data in Figure 4C.

claim: D18' is too short to enable WT-like Na+ permeation.
source: Moreover, single channel activity through E18'D channels was significantly reduced (Figure 4C), implying that D18' is too short to enable WT-like Na+ permeation
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the single channel data in Figure 4C.

claim: Single channel conductance in D21'N channels is similar to wild-type.
source: implying that D18' is too short to enable WT-like Na+ permeation (although single channel conductance was similar to WT in D21'N).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The need for precise positioning of E18' carboxylates might be a consequence of the formation of Na+-selective multi-carboxylate complexes during conduction.
source: We postulate that the need for such precise positioning of E18' carboxylates might be a consequence of the formation of Na+-selective multi-carboxylate complexes during conduction (e.g. Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a postulation based on the data.

claim: Each E18' contributes to selectivity in the ASIC trimer.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, each E18' contributes to selectivity, as even the 1/3 mutation decreases PNa+/PK+ and PNa+/PCs+ ratios.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by concatemeric channel data in Figure 4D.

claim: 1/3 E18'Q mutation maintains WT-like profile of PNa+ > PK+ > PCs+.
source: But while 1/3 maintained WT-like profile of PNa+ > PK+ > PCs+, it was only 2/3 and 3/3 where this profile collapsed
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by concatemeric channel data in Figure 4D.

claim: 2/3 and 3/3 E18'Q mutations cause the selectivity profile to collapse.
source: But while 1/3 maintained WT-like profile of PNa+ > PK+ > PCs+, it was only 2/3 and 3/3 where this profile collapsed, consistent with the cooperative interactions with ions suggested by simulations (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by concatemeric channel data in Figure 4D.

claim: The L7'A mutation causes no ostensible change in relative permeability in 1/3- or 2/3-mutated concatemeric channels.
source: In contrast, the L7'A mutation, which abolished selectivity in regular channels, caused no ostensible change in relative permeability in 1/3- or 2/3-mutated channels (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by concatemeric channel data in Figure 4D.

claim: The S12'A mutation renders regular channels non-functional.
source: Furthermore, the S12'A mutation rendered regular channels non-functional (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and had therefore eluded study.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stepwise introduction of S12'A mutation into concatemeric channels causes no change in relative permeability in 1/3- or 2/3-mutated channels.
source: However, a stepwise introduction of this mutation into concatemeric channels caused no change in relative permeability in 1/3- or 2/3-mutated channels
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by concatemeric channel data in Figure 4D.

claim: S12' makes little or no direct contribution to Na+ selectivity.
source: However, a stepwise introduction of this mutation into concatemeric channels caused no change in relative permeability in 1/3- or 2/3-mutated channels, providing novel functional evidence that S12' makes little or no direct contribution to Na+ selectivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the concatemeric channel data.

claim: The GAS belt is involved in reducing the barrier to K+ ions through backbone interactions.
source: Through experimental and computational approaches, we find that the GAS belt is involved in reducing the barrier to K+ ions through backbone interactions, but we find no evidence for Na+ selectivity occurring exclusively at this position.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and computational data.

claim: There is no evidence for Na+ selectivity occurring exclusively at the GAS belt.
source: Through experimental and computational approaches, we find that the GAS belt is involved in reducing the barrier to K+ ions through backbone interactions, but we find no evidence for Na+ selectivity occurring exclusively at this position.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and computational data.

claim: L7' and L14' on either side of the GAS belt are regions where selective Na+ conduction is controlled.
source: Our data identify other regions, including L7' and L14' on either side of the GAS belt, and especially E18' at the lower entrance to the pore, where selective Na+ conduction is most directly controlled.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: E18' at the lower entrance to the pore is where selective Na+ conduction is most directly controlled.
source: Our data identify other regions, including L7' and L14' on either side of the GAS belt, and especially E18' at the lower entrance to the pore, where selective Na+ conduction is most directly controlled.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The long-standing view that the GAS belt is the selectivity filter in ASICs needs to be rethought.
source: This prompts a rethinking of the long-standing view that the GAS belt is the selectivity filter in ASICs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The G10'C mutation adds a side chain to G10' and could indirectly alter the shape of the pore.
source: However, this mutation adds a side chain to G10', whose main chain carbonyl oxygen is implicated in conduction by structural data (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the G10'C mutation could indirectly alter the shape of the pore, as indeed Kellenberger et al. (1999a), suggested for GAS mutations in ENaCs.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The amide-ester main chain substitution at A11'α caused minimal structural consequences.
source: This caused minimal structural consequences, reflected in WT-like gating of A11'α channels (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The amide-ester substitution at A11'α decreased electrostatic potential around the G10' main chain carbonyl oxygen.
source: This caused minimal structural consequences, reflected in WT-like gating of A11'α channels (Figure 1C), yet decreased electrostatic potential around the G10' main chain carbonyl oxygen (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The A11'α alteration saw no effect on Na+ conductance but a modest decrease in apparent K+ permeability.
source: This alteration saw no effect on Na+ conductance but a modest decrease in apparent K+ permeability.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: MD simulations provide a good explanation for the effect of A11'α on K+ permeability.
source: Our MD simulations provide a good explanation for this effect.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation data.

claim: Na+ and K+ ions both fit through the GAS constriction.
source: Na+ and K+ ions both fit through the GAS constriction, but for K+ ions, this requires interaction with a G10' carbonyl in place of a water molecule (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For K+ ions to pass through the GAS constriction, interaction with a G10' carbonyl in place of a water molecule is required.
source: Na+ and K+ ions both fit through the GAS constriction, but for K+ ions, this requires interaction with a G10' carbonyl in place of a water molecule (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutant S12' concatemeric channels directly demonstrate that S12´ is unlikely to play a major role in ASIC selectivity.
source: Additionally, we used mutant S12' concatemeric channels to directly demonstrate that S12´ is unlikely to play a major role in ASIC selectivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the concatemeric channel data.

claim: The GAS belt may contribute to ion selectivity in ASICs, but is unlikely the site of the actual selectivity filter.
source: Thus, our experiments and simulations show that, while the GAS belt may contribute to ion selectivity in ASICs, it is unlikely the site of the actual selectivity filter, which we have demonstrated is located elsewhere in the pore, where mutations eliminate Na+ selectivity altogether.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and computational data.

claim: The actual selectivity filter is located elsewhere in the pore, where mutations eliminate Na+ selectivity altogether.
source: Thus, our experiments and simulations show that, while the GAS belt may contribute to ion selectivity in ASICs, it is unlikely the site of the actual selectivity filter, which we have demonstrated is located elsewhere in the pore, where mutations eliminate Na+ selectivity altogether.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and computational data.

claim: The loss of selectivity in the L14'A mutant could be an indirect effect on Na+ conduction caused by the loss of hydrophobic interactions between L14' side chains and adjacent helices.
source: We propose that the loss of selectivity in the L14'A mutant could be an indirect effect on Na+ conduction, caused by the loss of hydrophobic interactions between L14' side chains and adjacent helices (illustrated by Baconguis et al., 2014), which are likely retained in the more conservative L14'I mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on structural data.

claim: A role for the L14' side chain in maintaining the open channel structure is consistent with the effects of the L14'C mutation on channel gating.
source: Furthermore, a role for the L14' side chain in maintaining the open channel structure is also consistent with the effects of the L14'C mutation on channel gating (Carattino and Della Vecchia, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The L7' side chain is oriented toward adjacent helices in PDB:4NTW.
source: Similarly, the L7' side chain is oriented toward adjacent helices in PDB:4NTW (Baconguis et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to structural data.

claim: L7' is implicated in gating.
source: Similarly, the L7' side chain is oriented toward adjacent helices in PDB:4NTW (Baconguis et al., 2014) and is implicated in gating (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The L7'A mutation altered ASIC1a proton-gating more than any other mutant in the present study.
source: Indeed, in our hands the L7'A mutation altered ASIC1a proton-gating more than any other mutant in the present study (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: L7' might be important for pore conformation, without contributing to specific interactions with ions in the pore.
source: L7' might thus be important for pore conformation, without contributing to specific interactions with ions in the pore (consistent with the hydrophobic nature of the side chain).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: The closer proximity of adjacent helices in PDB:2QTS provides a means for carboxylate side chains to exert substantial control on selective binding at the channel opening to promote efficient multi-ion Na+ conduction.
source: Thus, although permeation is not observed in simulations with the closed-channel 2QTS, the closer proximity of adjacent helices provides a means for carboxylate side chains to exert substantial control on selective binding at the channel opening to promote efficient multi-ion Na+ conduction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation data.

claim: E18' is highly conserved in the DEG/ENaC family.
source: As E18' is highly conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations at the equivalent position to E18' in ENaCs reduce Na+ currents.
source: and mutations at the equivalent position in ENaCs reduce Na+ currents (Langloh et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: E18' likely controls Na+ conduction throughout the broader ENaC/DEG family.
source: it is foreseeable that E18' controls Na+ conduction throughout the broader ENaC/DEG family.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on conservation and functional data.

claim: ENaCs show substantially greater Na+ selectivity than ASICs.
source: As ENaCs show substantially greater Na+ selectivity than ASICs (e.g. Gründer and Pusch, 2015), however, significant differences must occur between these two examples of ENaC/DEG channels.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: G10' might be oriented differently in ENaCs such that it cannot provide the favorable backbone contribution to K+ conduction observed for ASICs.
source: We speculate that G10' might be oriented differently in ENaCs, such that it cannot provide the favorable backbone contribution to K+ conduction that we observed for ASICs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation.

claim: ENaCs possess E18' and E21' whereas ASICs possess E18' and D21'.
source: Moreover, in the selectivity filter we have identified, ENaCs possess E18' and E21' (whereas ASICs possess E18' and D21').
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The longer E21' side chain in ENaCs could help in the formation of cooperative multi-ion complexes, which could further increase Na+ selectivity.
source: The longer E21' side chain in ENaCs could help in the formation of cooperative multi-ion complexes, which could further increase Na+ selectivity, as suggested in our simulations with a narrower pore than that seen in PDB:4NTW.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on simulation data.

claim: The D21'E mutation in ASICs did not increase selectivity.
source: As we did not observe an increase in selectivity with D21'E mutant ASICs, we speculate that other factors govern the additional increase in selectivity in ENaCs, possibly by an even more narrow selectivity filter.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The combined experimental and computational approach reveals that main chain carbonyl oxygens at the levels of L7' and the GAS belt contribute to selectivity by interacting with permeating K+ ions.
source: Our combined experimental and computational approach reveals that although main chain carbonyl oxygens at the levels of L7' and the GAS belt contribute to selectivity by interacting with permeating K+ ions, the notion of the GAS belt as the ASIC selectivity filter must be revised.

claim: A selectivity filter comprised of E18´and D21´ at the lower end of the ASIC1a pore discriminates ions based on interactions with a band of carboxylate side chains.
source: Our data clearly describe a selectivity filter (comprised of E18´and D21´) at the lower end of the ASIC1a pore, which discriminates ions based on interactions with a band of carboxylate side chains.
